We are going to do the interview with Helen Humes for the Oral History Project, and this is Helen Oakley Dance doing it. It's May 12th, 1981. We'll see what we've got.
Helen, let's get a shot on your voice. Tell me - what we're going to do is, we're going to start right in the beginning.
Okay.
Alright? You're going to tell me about your parents.

Well, if you want me to start there, alright. Well, I had the best parents in the world, I'll say that, because they were. Well, my mother used to be a school teacher and my father, he was, well in the earlier days he was a railroad man, and then he went to law school and he studied to be an attorney. And then in the later years he was a real estate man.
Helen, about your father being an attorney, wasn't that a little unusual in those days?
Yes it was a little unusual especially in the South. But he was one of the first black attorneys in Louieville.

I don't know.
When we talked about it you thought probably your father was born in about 1978.
Not nineteen.
I know he died in 1975 and if he had lived until July he would have been 97. But he died in January, January 3rd. I suppose he was 96 1/2.
Was members of his family, were they all long lived people? Did they have long lives?
Well, I didn't know too much about them. I knew I had a cousin. Her name was Mildred. And then I had an Uncle Ed. But they all died, you know, they died when I was young.
When you were young.
Yes. And I didn't know too much about them.
Well your father certainly had a long life.
Oh yes, he did.

Yeah, she didn't work.

She stayed home and pitted me. She used to get up and she'd say, come on lazy. It's be summertime, you know, and she said, baby I got us some sherbert made and you could come on and get some, or if it's too hot. So I'd get up. Yeah.
It was the three of you.
And then after I left home I used to come home every year, two or three times a year, so I could take Mama to play bingo. We'd go to the races. We lived, you know, just a couple of blocks from the

Yes, from Churchill Downs.

So we just enjoyed ourselves. I guess I had an unusual home life because we were just so happy. And I never heard my mother and father argue. The first time I heard my father curse, he was in the hospital, after I put him in this hospital, and one of the male nurses came out and they tried to make him do something. Papa said, 'what damn man nurses - tend to his business'. And that's the first time I heard him curse.

Oh yes, he used to go. But sometimes we'd run off on him there because we didn't know he was going to be there, you know. And I'd be walking around down there and I'd run into Papa.
So this is how you got your little taste for the races.
Yeah. We were just into it ourselves.

segments.title: Copyright notice, title page and start of the 1981 interview
segments.summary: Rutgers IJS copyright warnings and title page, then Helen Oakley Dance opens the May 12, 1981 Oral History Project interview and asks Humes to begin with her parents.

segments.title: Her parents: teacher mother, father a railroad man turned lawyer
segments.summary: Humes describes her mother the school teacher and her father, a railroad man who studied law and became one of Louisville's first black attorneys, then a real estate man. He died in 1975 near age 97; she recalls few other relatives.

segments.title: Happy home life, her mother at home and trips to Churchill Downs
segments.summary: Her mother stayed home and spoiled her with sherbet, popcorn and taffy. The family lived near Churchill Downs and went to the races together, and she never heard her parents argue.

segments.title: Growing up next to Ann Street Baptist Church
segments.summary: The family lived next door to Ann Street Baptist Church, with Sunday School, the eleven o'clock service and the evening B.Y.P.U. taking up most of Sunday.

segments.title: Singing at the piano as a small child and early lessons
segments.summary: Her mother sang in the choir and played piano at home while Humes sang along. Humes sang at church concerts at three or four, had a German teacher and then a lady teacher, and stopped lessons early. John Hammond later advised her against voice study.

segments.title: Miss Bess Allen's orphans home school and its music pupils
segments.summary: Bess Allen ran an orphans home with an evening summer music school where Lockwood Lewis taught any instrument. Humes names fellow pupils Dicky Wells, Jonah Jones, Charles Blumer and drummer Bill Beeson.

segments.title: Her father 'Judge': generous, kindly and strict
segments.summary: People called her father 'Judge' because he was always at the courthouse. Humes says she resembles him, that her only-child home was open to friends without fathers, and that both parents were strict about school dances.

segments.title: Derby Day parties at home and visitors sent to her parents
segments.summary: Every Derby Day the family held an all-day party with food, cards and checkers and watched the horses from the back field. Later she sent friends she met while travelling to visit her parents in Kentucky.

segments.title: Taking four years off her age when she came to New York
segments.summary: Musicians told her to lie about her age in New York, so she gave 1913 although she was born June 23, 1909. Books repeat 1913, and people today do not believe her real age.

segments.title: Big bands that came to Louisville, and trying to recall one
segments.summary: Her father drove her and her friends to dances when the big bands came to town. She recalls Earl Hines and Duke Ellington, met Lunceford only later in Buffalo, knew Fletcher and Horace Henderson, and cannot place the band Dance is asking about.

segments.title: Central High and the Center School: Dicky Wells, Jonah Jones and friends
segments.summary: All the future musicians attended Central High and gathered at Miss Allen's Center School. Humes remembers them as funny, ordinary schoolmates, and she and Dance try and fail to recall the name of Jonah Jones's brother-in-law and wife.

segments.title: Bessie Allen and her saxophonist son George Allen
segments.summary: Bessie Allen headed the orphans home. Her son George was a professional saxophonist for a long time and, Humes believes, now lives in Georgia.

segments.title: Trying clarinet and trumpet, then the marching band and club dances
segments.summary: Humes quit clarinet and trumpet quickly and stayed with singing and piano. Miss Bess took her marching band to fairs, and at night Humes played piano and sang at the dance, where the band played popular songs and jazz.

segments.title: Singing with megaphones and her powerful voice
segments.summary: Without microphones, bands used megaphones, which Humes thinks explains why she sings so loud. She credits God for her voice and has no explanation for her breath control.

segments.title: Never listening to her own records
segments.summary: Humes never plays her own records and always feels they could have been better, though she hears playbacks in the studio and asks to sing again.

segments.chapter: Central High, first records and leaving home
segments.title: The little school band, her boyfriend Sprat Morton and Bill Beason
segments.summary: After the tape turns over, she describes how tight the little band was. Her childhood boyfriend was trumpeter Bernise 'Sprat' Morton, who later played with Roy Eldridge in Horace Henderson's band but got no farther than Buffalo; drummer Bill Beason later played with Chick Webb.

segments.chapter: Central High, first records and leaving home
segments.title: Sylvester Weaver hears her at the Palace Theatre and brings Tommy Rockwell
segments.summary: At thirteen or fourteen, playing piano and singing with the band at the Palace movie theatre, Humes was heard by blues guitarist Sylvester Weaver, who knew her father and brought record man Tommy Rockwell to hear her at home.

segments.chapter: Central High, first records and leaving home
segments.title: Her first record date and being cast as a young blues singer
segments.summary: Her mother took her to make the first records, with suggestive blues lyrics such as 'Do What You Did Last Night' and a race track number. She had not thought of herself as a blues singer and prefers ballads.

segments.chapter: Central High, first records and leaving home
segments.title: Selling the family piano and getting rid of her music after her mother died
segments.summary: She describes singing on the porch as a girl, then how after her mother passed she sold the upright piano for $10 and discarded records, a Basie-gift record player and music. Dance defers the subject.

segments.chapter: Central High, first records and leaving home
segments.title: Rockwell wants her on tour, her mother insists she finish school
segments.summary: Rockwell wanted to send her on tour but her mother said she would finish school first. Humes had no wish to travel after hearing how musicians were treated, and the family and the little band were proud of her records.

segments.chapter: Central High, first records and leaving home
segments.title: The boys go north; her 1934 visit to Buffalo and first singing at the Spiderweb
segments.summary: The school band members left Louisville for Cleveland and Buffalo. Just out of high school, she visited Luke Stewart and his wife in Buffalo and was pushed to sing at the Spiderweb with Al Sears's band, her first New York State appearance with a microphone.

segments.title: Not planning a music career: bank secretary and the Merry Cottage
segments.summary: Her father wanted her in his business and she had no career plan. She worked as a secretary at a liberal Louisville bank, then loved waitressing at the Merry Cottage, where she arranged flowers and met nice people.

segments.title: Stuff Smith's band at the Hotel Vendome in Buffalo
segments.summary: Luke Stewart, Jonah Jones and Tom played at the Hotel Vendome in Buffalo in a band with Stuff Smith, whose violin and singing she admired. She also praises violinist Ginger Smock.

segments.title: Getting hired to sing at the Vendome and dressing from thrift shops
segments.summary: The hotel hired her to sing with the home-town musicians. Worried about having no clothes, she bought gowns at thrift shops and impressed Mrs. Clore with her wardrobe.

segments.title: Songs she sang with the Vendome band, including 'I'm In Love With You'
segments.summary: She sang 'If I Could Be With You', 'Trouble in Mind' and 'Blue Because Of You', and recites the lines of 'I'm In Love With You', which she never recorded. She liked the band improvising behind her.

segments.title: Who was in the Vendome band: Stuff Smith, Jonah Jones, Luke Stewart
segments.summary: Stuff Smith had the band at the Vendome, with Jonah Jones and Luke Stewart. Dicky Wells had already gone to New York, and she and Stuff did no comedy duets in those days.

segments.title: Albany: cooking for musicians at Charlie Miller's restaurant
segments.summary: From Buffalo she went to Albany and worked in Charlie Miller's restaurant, cooking red beans, rice and spareribs for the musicians who packed the place. She later cooked for the Basie band in theatre dressing rooms.

segments.title: Seeing Billie Holiday at the Big Apple, and what she thought of her
segments.summary: Friends from Albany drove her to New York to hear Billie Holiday at the Big Apple, where she saw Billie pull up her dress to collect money. Humes says it was not her style but remembers Billie as a lovely, harmless person who once got her into a locked dressing room.

segments.title: 'Ebobaleeba' and 'Million Dollar Secret': hits and credit disputes
segments.summary: Humes and Dance sort out the late-1940s hits. 'Ebobaleeba' was her only royalty; 'Million Dollar Secret' for Modern was recorded at the Shrine, and the recording man put his name on it until Mr. Koenig got it removed.

segments.title: Spending the royalties on a house next to the old church, and her tenants
segments.summary: From $3,500 in royalties she kept $500 and sent $3,000 home. Her father bought the lot of the church next door and they built a rental house, where she keeps the rent at $65 a month for elderly tenants.

segments.title: 'Simply Heavenly' and her voice in movies and television
segments.summary: She played in a short-run stage show of Langston Hughes's 'Simply Heavenly', and her voice was used in films such as 'Panic in the Streets', 'My Blue Heaven' and 'The Steel Trap', though she never watched them. She did hear the television 'Come Home Bill Bailey'.

segments.title: Her sister books her to Australia with Red Norvo
segments.summary: Working in San Francisco, Humes was told by her sister Dorothy that she had been booked for Australia with Red Norvo and had to go. She mentions friendship with Mildred Bailey and Norvo's wife Eve.

segments.title: Sounding like Billie Holiday, Mildred Bailey and Ella
segments.summary: People say she sounds like Billie, Mildred Bailey or Ella. Dance notes Stanley Dance's point that Humes's early blues records were compared to Mildred before Bailey had recorded.

segments.title: The long first flight to Australia with Red Norvo's trio
segments.summary: In 1952 the slow little plane stopped at Fiji. Red Norvo brought a bass and guitar player; the guitarist later died in a fire, which Norvo's wife wrote to tell her.

segments.title: Three more Australian tours and love of the country
segments.summary: The first tour lasted about two weeks. Later she returned alone for eight weeks, then ten months, and was offered citizenship, which she declined while her parents lived. She went back in the early 1960s.

segments.title: A slow period in Los Angeles and work at Gene Norman's club
segments.summary: After Australia she stayed in Los Angeles through a quiet stretch, working now and then at a big club that Gene Norman bought and renamed.

segments.title: Her brief marriage to Harlan O. Smith of the Navy
segments.summary: Humes reluctantly tells of marrying Harlan Smith, a Navy man, in Reno. He wrote every day, she tired of writing back, and the marriage faded when his ship left.

segments.title: The Contemporary session with Benny Carter, Shelly Manne and Andre Previn
segments.summary: Dance recalls 'They Raided the Joint' and 'I Cried for You', then the Contemporary album Humes calls one of her best sessions, with Benny Carter finding the musicians. Previn later asked, through Koenig, to be on her next date.

segments.title: The 1960 string session and the 1961 date with Wynton Kelly
segments.summary: She enjoyed her first session with strings in 1960, with Ben Webster, and a 1961 date with Wynton Kelly and Teddy Edwards. She says a good piano player means she is in business.

segments.title: The Jazzology album with Connie Berry
segments.summary: She made a small Jazzology album with pianist Connie Berry in a studio, which Humes says sounded as though it had been put together wrong. She still has a copy.

segments.title: Her first European trip: the 1962 blues festival
segments.summary: In 1962 she went to Europe on a blues festival with T-Bone Walker, Memphis Slim and Willie Dixon. She notes she does not sing the blues constantly, and a Swedish pianist backed her very well.

segments.title: Back in Los Angeles: Shelly's Manne-Hole and Redd Foxx's club
segments.summary: After France she worked from Shelly Manne's Manne-Hole as home base, then at Redd Foxx's club. She returned from her third Australian tour in 1965 and learned her mother was sick.

segments.title: Returning to Louisville to nurse her parents and giving up music
segments.summary: Both parents were sick, so she went home. After her mother died she got rid of her piano, records and music and said she would not sing any more.

segments.title: Taking a job at the munitions plant
segments.summary: Thinking her career over, she drove elderly women to bingo. One drove her to a munitions plant and talked her into the hiring line, and she got the job after a doctor's check and a strike.

segments.chapter: Europe and the Black and Blue years
segments.title: European fans: loyal and generous
segments.summary: Starting on fans, Humes says European audiences are completely in your corner. In Sweden everything was paid for, and a driver and chauffeur looked after her.

segments.chapter: Europe and the Black and Blue years
segments.title: Sweden in 1980: Bo Stenhammer's festival
segments.summary: Bo Stenhammer booked her for a Swedish festival with a good band behind her. It was her only Swedish trip, in 1980, soon after her illness, and the organisers bent over backwards.

segments.chapter: Europe and the Black and Blue years
segments.title: Swedish concerts, TV show and working with local musicians
segments.summary: She did a TV show and two club concerts, closing the show as the only American star. She brings no band or scores, only lead sheets, and the European musicians are excellent.

segments.chapter: Europe and the Black and Blue years
segments.title: Hotel treatment in Sweden and keeping some privacy
segments.summary: Hosts took her to meals and tipped for her; she tipped her maid and clerks. She says she gets privacy by telling people not to call before a certain time, but otherwise just grins and bears it.

segments.chapter: Europe and the Black and Blue years
segments.title: Dr. and Madame Chavron: her favourite family in France
segments.summary: The Chavrons of Orange, France, kept open house for musicians with food, a pool, records and film clips. They paid her hotel bills and she regards the family as home. She was upset to hear Madame Chavron had died.

segments.chapter: Europe and the Black and Blue years
segments.title: A writer's family in France; first trips in 1962, 1973 and 1975
segments.summary: She mentions another French family headed by a writer, met at George Wein's 1975 festival. She dates her first French trip to 1973 for Black and Blue, after the 1962 blues festival.

segments.chapter: Europe and the Black and Blue years
segments.title: The 1972-73 Black and Blue session with Jay McShann and Milt Buckner
segments.summary: After the Basie tribute Stanley Dance arranged, she was in France five days later, touring for Monestier and recording 'Helen Comes Back' with Jay McShann and Milt Buckner. Dance praises McShann's range beyond blues piano.

segments.chapter: Europe and the Black and Blue years
segments.title: Milt Buckner's death and his health
segments.summary: A caller from Switzerland checked on her health. They discuss Milt Buckner's heart attack after trouble lifting his organ gear, his marriage to Monestier's wife, and Dr. Chavron's blood tests that revealed his high blood pressure and diabetes.

segments.chapter: Europe and the Black and Blue years
segments.title: Musicians who need a drink to work: Jay McShann
segments.summary: Humes grows disgusted when Jay McShann gets drinking, though he still plays wonderfully. Dance laments how many musicians harm themselves this way.

segments.chapter: Europe and the Black and Blue years
segments.title: Scott Hamilton and the night he drank at her gig in New Orleans
segments.summary: Humes admires young Scott Hamilton but scolded him about drinking. In New Orleans he drank through a televised fight, reeled on the stand, apologised and promised it would not happen again.

segments.chapter: Europe and the Black and Blue years
segments.title: Copying the old lifestyle: a young singer imitating Billie Holiday's drinking
segments.summary: Dance says Hamilton copied the 1930s lifestyle. Humes tells a young woman singer who fell off a bar stool and said 'Billie Holiday drank' that she need not pattern herself on Billie; Benny Goodman gave that singer her start.

segments.chapter: Europe and the Black and Blue years
segments.title: Monestier and Tamadjian: touring and studios of Black and Blue
segments.summary: Monestier and his partner Tamadjian promote tours and concerts together. Humes sometimes rode the bus with the musicians. She notes Monestier's pretended lack of understanding and cannot say whether the studio is in Bordeaux or Paris.

segments.chapter: Europe and the Black and Blue years
segments.title: Why Black and Blue records are good but pay no royalties
segments.summary: Dance admires how Black and Blue records unsaleable artists on good tours, but Humes says they send no royalties. She mentions a Hot Club of France award.

segments.chapter: Europe and the Black and Blue years
segments.title: Hugues Panassie and his wife follow her tours
segments.summary: Panassie and his wife Natalie always turned up wherever she sang in France, and Panassie marveled that even young people loved her and wanted her to keep singing. The text is broken by an out-of-order page.

segments.title: Back to Louisville, then the Cotton Club in Cincinnati with Al Sears's band
segments.summary: Homesick after Albany, she went home and then took a job at the Cotton Club in a Cincinnati hotel. Her band there was Al Sears's, whom she knew from Buffalo, with pianist Bugs Roberts from Kentucky.

segments.title: Count Basie offers $35 a week; later she joins and meets John Hammond
segments.summary: Basie heard her at the Cotton Club and offered $35 a week to replace Billie Holiday. She declined, then later travelled with his band to New York, where she sang at the Renaissance Ballroom and John Hammond heard her.

segments.title: First New York session and rowing in Central Park
segments.summary: Her first New York session was with Harry James. She had only visited New York for a day to hear Billie, and when she came with Al Sears she rented a rowboat in Central Park by herself.

segments.title: Her New York apartment and romances: Sprat and Al
segments.summary: She lived in an apartment on 117th Street, doing some 'heavy rooming'. Asked about romance, she says Sprat visited her in Buffalo and Albany, nobody was around in Cincinnati, and in New York there was only Al.

segments.title: Her second Tommy Rockwell session in New York
segments.summary: Humes recalls that her second session for Rockwell was made in New York, when she stayed with friends and went with Mr. and Mrs. Weaver.

segments.title: The Harry James session with Basie men and John Hammond
segments.summary: Harry James, then with Benny Goodman, used Basie sidemen for her first New York date. The titles included 'The Song of the Wanderer', and Dance gives the personnel. Humes calls it the only session she really enjoyed.

segments.title: The Apollo amateur contest that led to the Basie band
segments.summary: At the Apollo amateur contest to find a Basie singer, Humes came second to a girl who sounded like Ella but could not rehearse without records. The band then asked Humes to try, and Basie said he had asked her first.

segments.title: Basie band pay and laughing on the bandstand
segments.summary: Pay started at $35, rose to $50 and $75 and reached about $125. Humes and Jimmy Rushing joked on the bandstand until Basie sent them to the dressing room.

segments.title: Recording with Basie and Jimmy Rushing in California, released years later
segments.summary: After Basie left, he visited her in California and they made a session that Columbia only released recently, after her Muse album with Eddie Vinson. She also did an earlier session with Jimmy Rushing.

segments.title: Living on the bus as the only woman, 'like a little sister'
segments.summary: She had never travelled with a band. Living on the bus as the only woman was a big experience, and the men treated her as a little sister while she sewed buttons and fixed lunches.

segments.title: Band personalities, dice on the bus and card games
segments.summary: Sweets was funny, and Lester Young and Vic Dickenson rolled dice on the bus and were first to go broke. She loaned them money, played tonk and poker, and won against men who thought she did not know how.

segments.title: One-nighters in the South, Earle Warren on the train and Basie's bridges
segments.summary: One-nighters through the South were rough. Light-skinned Earle Warren was told to leave the white coach, and later got food for the band in segregated towns. Basie would get off the bus to walk across rickety bridges.

segments.title: Dressing up for Southern audiences and her view of race
segments.summary: She kept evening dresses on the bus to look nice for audiences, which people said other singers did not. Dance asks about dances split by race; Humes says she never thought about color, since her father dealt with white realtors on equal terms.

segments.title: Her relationship with Basie and Al Killian's wedding
segments.summary: Humes says she was not Basie's girlfriend right away and it never got serious. Basie visited her mother's house in Louisville and once asked about being a son-in-law, but she saw him as only a pleasant companion.

segments.title: Catherine Basie and leaving the road after four years
segments.summary: Basie's wife Catherine, formerly burlesque queen Blondie Scott of Cleveland, never spoke to Humes and it did not bother her. After about four years Humes had enough of the road.

segments.chapter: After Basie: Cafe Society to Los Angeles
segments.title: Leaving Basie when the band wanted Lena Horne
segments.summary: Dance moves to the Basie recordings, then asks whether Basie tried to keep her. Humes says the band was trying to get Lena Horne, so she left.

segments.chapter: After Basie: Cafe Society to Los Angeles
segments.title: Cafe Society, the Famous Door and the Village Vanguard
segments.summary: After a spell at home, John Hammond called her to Cafe Society, where she worked with Meade Lux Lewis, Albert Ammons, Pete Johnson, Art Tatum, Teddy Wilson, Ed Hall and Sid Catlett. She also played the Famous Door with George Shearing's group, and Bricktop was across the street.

segments.chapter: After Basie: Cafe Society to Los Angeles
segments.title: Singing with Teddy Wilson and Art Tatum, and Andre Previn again
segments.summary: Humes felt lucky to sing with great pianists. She calls Teddy Wilson the perfect accompanist, says Tatum played so much she wanted just to listen, and repeats the Previn story from the Contemporary sessions.

segments.chapter: After Basie: Cafe Society to Los Angeles
segments.title: The man who asked if she was colored
segments.summary: A man called her out at Cafe Society to ask if she was colored, saying he had seen her picture and did not know. When she answered, he froze and apologised.

segments.chapter: After Basie: Cafe Society to Los Angeles
segments.title: The Village Vanguard with Eddie Heywood, and Pearl Bailey as her fill-in
segments.summary: At the Vanguard with Eddie Heywood, she went home for Derby time and found Pearl Bailey to cover. Pearl got her big break at the Blue Angel and also worked briefly for Basie.

segments.chapter: After Basie: Cafe Society to Los Angeles
segments.title: Her parents' pride and open house at Derby time
segments.summary: Her parents were proud but sorry she was away so much, and visited her. Each Derby time the family home held open house for people from everywhere.

segments.chapter: After Basie: Cafe Society to Los Angeles
segments.title: 1944: a package show to New Orleans and teaming with pianist Connie Berry
segments.summary: Dance recalls the package tour south and west in 1944. Humes teamed with Atlanta pianist Connie Berry, who had played two pianos with Joe Turner and for Gladys Bentley. They worked clubs in California, sometimes booked by Joe Glaser.

segments.chapter: After Basie: Cafe Society to Los Angeles
segments.title: Staying at the Dunbar Hotel and her friendship with Ivy Anderson
segments.summary: On first coming to Los Angeles she used the Dunbar Hotel as headquarters, then stayed with various people. She became good friends with Ivy Anderson, played cards with her and sang at her funeral.

segments.chapter: After Basie: Cafe Society to Los Angeles
segments.title: Card games in Los Angeles and the night of the raid
segments.summary: Women in Los Angeles played blackjack, tonk and bingo-like games constantly. At a game she co-hosted with a singer named Helen on 43rd Street, the police under Mayor Bradley raided it; they paid $5 and resumed for two days.

segments.chapter: After Basie: Cafe Society to Los Angeles
segments.title: Streets of Paris and the girl group with Nina Russell and Ginger Smock
segments.summary: She worked six or eight weeks at the Streets of Paris on Hollywood Boulevard, also with Red Norvo. She describes a group of organist Nina Russell, pianist Maida and violinist Ginger Smock, and says Russell now lives in Hungry Horse, Montana.

segments.chapter: Jazz at the Philharmonic and life on the road
segments.title: Joining Jazz at the Philharmonic through Mary McKay
segments.summary: Mary McKay talked Norman Granz into letting Humes sing at an opera house concert in 1945-46, and she became a regular on the JATP tours. She and Granz and Lester Young were also supposed to go into the record business together.

segments.chapter: Jazz at the Philharmonic and life on the road
segments.title: The Gene Norman Shrine concert of 'Ebobaleeba'
segments.summary: She did not know what Gene Norman did with the Shrine recording, which became a big hit. They try to sort out who was on it; the page is followed by a stray fragment of the Panassie quote.

segments.chapter: Jazz at the Philharmonic and life on the road
segments.title: American fans and keeping her cool in noisy rooms
segments.summary: At the New Orleans Hyatt-Regency, Dance marveled at her patience with talkative crowds and fans. Humes just smiles, gives autographs, and says she loves people.

segments.chapter: Jazz at the Philharmonic and life on the road
segments.title: Giving the audience your best: 'the old school'
segments.summary: Dance contrasts Ellington and Hines, who felt they owed the audience a show, with later musicians who felt the audience owed them. Humes says she is from the old school and always does her best.

segments.chapter: Jazz at the Philharmonic and life on the road
segments.title: Favourite rooms and the Johns Manville jazz parties in Denver
segments.summary: She liked the Hyatt hotels in New Orleans and Indianapolis. Johns Manville's president Mr. Goodwin held annual jazz parties in Denver where she got a huge suite, a limousine and catered parties.

segments.chapter: Jazz at the Philharmonic and life on the road
segments.title: Disneyworld townhouse and bassist Louise Davis
segments.summary: At Disneyworld they give her a two-storey townhouse and a car for a two-week stay. She takes only her pianist and works with bassist Louise Davis, whom Dance met in New Orleans.

segments.chapter: Jazz at the Philharmonic and life on the road
segments.title: Gambling on cards: Los Angeles games and JATP travel
segments.summary: When she arrived in Los Angeles people played blackjack, poker and pinochle for hundreds of dollars for days. On JATP tours she, Flip Phillips and Roy Eldridge played cards on trains and planes, and she enjoyed travelling with men.

segments.chapter: Jazz at the Philharmonic and life on the road
segments.title: Cruises and the Rotterdam trip with Carmen, Dizzy and Earl
segments.summary: On a cruise the entertainers played bingo and cards in the afternoons. Humes loves cruises because she works only one day and can enjoy the rest.

segments.chapter: Jazz at the Philharmonic and life on the road
segments.title: 'Life has been very nice to me': no soap opera stories
segments.summary: Dance quotes a Leonard Feather piece saying Humes would not give dramatics. Humes says she remembers only good things, with no drugs, just bingo, cards and meeting people.

segments.chapter: Jazz at the Philharmonic and life on the road
segments.title: Dizzy and Babs Gonzales rehearsing at her Douglas House apartment
segments.summary: Around 1944 she lived at the Douglas House in New York, and Dizzy Gillespie, Babs Gonzales and others rehearsed and ate at her place. She cooked and told them to clean up after themselves.

segments.chapter: Jazz at the Philharmonic and life on the road
segments.title: Dizzy Gillespie the man, and his book
segments.summary: They agree Dizzy is funny and warm-hearted and helps young musicians. Dance thought his book a little controversial; Humes was given a copy but has not read it.

segments.chapter: Jazz at the Philharmonic and life on the road
segments.title: Working with Charlie Parker
segments.summary: Dizzy's friends in the 1940s weren't yet on their own. Humes recorded with Charlie Parker and found him fine, playing blues and everything; after hearing the Basie boys he did not strike her as strange.

segments.title: Herschel Evans and the Lester Young rivalry
segments.summary: Humes calls Herschel Evans one of the great ones and agrees with Dance that the supposed rivalry with Lester Young was not real, and that Herschel was a sweet man.

segments.title: Dicky Wells, 'Fat Fanny' and the Basie band as a happy family
segments.summary: Dicky Wells greeted her in the band, and Earle Warren and others called her 'Fat Fanny'. She describes the band as a big happy family with Basie as the nicest boss, who never used authority.

segments.title: Funny moments: Vic Dickenson in Brooklyn and Walter Page at the Apollo
segments.summary: In Brooklyn a high Vic Dickenson started playing after the band ended and the band backed him with riffs. At the Apollo Walter Page fell off the stand but kept holding up the bass.

segments.title: Basie's piano playing: 'what they wanted to hear'
segments.summary: Dance says Basie pretended to be embarrassed about not playing much piano. Humes says he played what the audience wanted to hear and could play more if he wished.

segments.title: Did Basie drop sick sidemen? A rumor Humes rejects
segments.summary: Dance relays stories that Basie let a sick Charlie Fowlkes go while he was in hospital. Humes had never heard it and doubts Basie would have done it himself.

segments.title: Seeing Basie in Pasadena, and the band's care for him
segments.summary: She saw Basie from across the stage in Pasadena and he sent word to her. Dance relays Bobby Plater's account that the band, sober and on the ball, carried the ailing Basie up theatre stairs on a European tour.

segments.title: Tipping and giving: Humes's generosity
segments.summary: At the Hyatt in New Orleans she tipped all the staff. Dance reveals she sent $100 checks in Christmas cards. Humes says she likes doing things for people and thinks it comes back double.

segments.title: Loyal American fans and friends: Jim Blackman and the Bittemans
segments.summary: Jim Blackman and Paul Lentz are devoted white fans from New Orleans. Mr. and Mrs. Bitteman in New York are like family, and their daughter Tina in France looks after festival people.

segments.title: After 1973 and Alberta Hunter's 'not bitchy enough' advice
segments.summary: Dance says the 1973 comeback showed more of Humes than her R&B hits. Humes recounts Alberta Hunter telling her she was not bitchy enough and stories of Hunter and another singer rebuking talkative audiences.

segments.title: Henry Pleasants's review of her late-career singing
segments.summary: Dance reads Henry Pleasants's praise of the album 'It's All Over Town' comparing her to Ethel Waters, Fanny Brice and Peggy Lee. Dance notes such writing was absent in the fifties.

segments.title: Contemporary Records and Lester Koenig's lack of promotion
segments.summary: Humes loved Contemporary and Mr. Koenig but says he never pushed the records beyond sending copies to disc jockeys. She thinks they were her best work; Nat Hentoff and Koenig wrote notes, and Previn, Marty Paich and Wynton Kelly played.

segments.title: Racism: Norman Granz insisting on hotels and train service
segments.summary: Humes says she has not had trouble with racism and wonders why. Norman Granz made hotels that excluded Black guests accept the JATP company and got the best train accommodations, and she saw no friction among performers.

segments.title: Redcap and airport restroom incidents
segments.summary: In Atlanta a Black redcap refused to put her in her drawing room until a white redcap did. In an airport she walked into the white restroom and told the attendant she would not leave without using it.

segments.title: The gas station restroom and the police
segments.summary: Driving with her cousin's family, she was refused a restroom at a Southern gas station. The owner called the police, and she told both off, saying she had asked for a restroom, not a certain color.

segments.title: Pianists: Dave McKenna and Red Balaban's group
segments.summary: Beginning a run through pianists, Dance names Dave McKenna, whom Humes worked with once at a college concert in the East. She also worked with Red Balaban's group.

segments.title: Jimmy Rowles: a favourite pianist who drinks
segments.summary: Rowles is one of her favourite pianists, though he drinks despite saying he does not. He now plays for Ella, and walked out on Alberta Hunter at the Cookery during intermission.

segments.title: Irene Kitchings, Teddy Wilson's first wife and composer
segments.summary: Dance reports that Irene Kitchings died last year. Humes planned to record her songs such as 'It's the Little Things That Mean So Much'. Dance recalls Irene's own group in Chicago and then raises Roger Kellaway.

segments.title: Sir Charles Thompson: plans to work together
segments.summary: Humes is alive and in Zurich and plans to use Sir Charles Thompson at the Cookery. He is sometimes touchy with the band, she advises him to just go along, and she notes people must go to Europe to get big.

segments.title: Ram Ramirez, songwriter and pianist
segments.summary: Humes made a session with Ram Ramirez, who writes beautiful songs, can play when he wants, and is temperamental but nice.

segments.title: Horace and Fletcher Henderson, and Ellington as accompanist
segments.summary: Dance compares Horace Henderson's piano with Fletcher's simple style. She relays Cootie Williams calling Ellington the greatest accompanist, and Humes agrees an accompanist must anticipate the singer.

segments.title: Ellis Larkins: great accompanist, temperamental
segments.summary: Humes calls Ellis Larkins one of the greatest but difficult; he would not follow her tempos and sings while playing. He accompanied her when she returned to the Cookery and on her first comeback album with George Benson.

segments.title: Her pianist Jerry and his stage seizures
segments.summary: Her current pianist Jerry stopped drinking on doctor's orders. She describes a concert in Chicago where he stopped playing, and says he has something like seizures.

segments.title: Bobby Short and his cousin Rudy
segments.summary: Humes praises Bobby Short as a performer. His cousin Rudy, once Debbie Reynolds's musical director, worked with her at the Tiffany Club in Los Angeles. Dance says the Los Angeles years are undocumented.

segments.title: Women pianists: Mary Lou Williams, Connie Berry, Nellie Lutcher, Rose Murphy
segments.summary: Humes names Mary Lou Williams as the greatest and lists Connie Berry, Nellie Lutcher and Rose Murphy as favourite pianists. Rose Murphy and Major Holley went to Ronnie Scott's after Humes.

segments.title: Camille Howard from the 'Million Dollar Secret' record
segments.summary: Camille Howard, who worked with Roy Milton and played on Humes's 'Million Dollar Secret' record, has reportedly retired for religious reasons. Humes was looking for her and thinks a woman pianist would be fun.

segments.title: Ray Charles, James P. Johnson and Lil Armstrong's 'Brown Girl'
segments.summary: Humes says Ray Charles is in a class by himself with real blues. Her first record was with James P. Johnson, whom she barely remembers. She plans to sing Lil Armstrong's 'Brown Girl' and recites it.

segments.title: Louis Armstrong, Velma Middleton and the Newport tribute
segments.summary: She first heard Louis at a ballroom dance and calls him the greatest. She cannot recall what she sang at George Wein's televised Armstrong tribute, which also had Dizzy Gillespie.

segments.title: Billy Eckstine, Harry Belafonte, Billy Daniels and Pha Terrell
segments.summary: Humes praises Billy Eckstine, has never met Harry Belafonte, remembers working with Billy Daniels at the Famous Door, and plans to sing Pha Terrell's 'When the Real Thing Comes Along'.

segments.title: Cleo Laine, Sarah Vaughan, Ella and Peggy Lee as favourites
segments.summary: Humes first heard Cleo Laine in London but has not met her. Sarah Vaughan, Ella and Peggy Lee are her favourite singers.

segments.title: Ella Fitzgerald: too serious about her work
segments.summary: Humes jokes that Ella should retire from the Grammy competition. They agree Ella is conscientious to a fault, fusses and gets upset with sidemen, and Gus Johnson had to calm her down.

segments.title: Peggy Lee and how much of her came from Billie
segments.summary: Humes met Peggy Lee in California, who sang her baby to sleep with 'Ebobaleeba'. Dance says Peggy took much from Billie Holiday and made millions while Billie struggled; Humes shrugs that is the business.

segments.title: Marva Josie and doing what feels comfortable
segments.summary: Humes says Marva Josie would be better singing as she wants, not as a glamour girl. She herself never thinks about what others are doing and could sing rock if she wanted.

segments.title: Dorothy Donegan's overplaying attitude
segments.summary: Dorothy Donegan, she says, is the best piano player but tries to outdo everyone and shake and show herself, which makes her unpopular. Humes advises her to just sit and play and smile.

segments.title: Nat Cole, the 'sugar pie'
segments.summary: Humes recalls Nat Cole as a nice person who deserved his success, although Dance regrets that he played less piano as he became successful.

segments.title: Mildred Bailey, Connie Boswell, Maxine Sullivan and Betty Carter
segments.summary: People say Humes sounds like Mildred Bailey. She liked Connie Boswell and Maxine Sullivan, and first heard Betty Carter when they sang on the same concert several years ago.

segments.title: Church music, Mahalia Jackson and not mixing gospel with club work
segments.summary: Humes dislikes modern church music that sounds like rock and roll. She admires Marion Williams and met Mahalia Jackson in Chicago around 1939-40, and does not think church songs belong in club work.

segments.title: Her vocal range, lyrics and listening to the piano
segments.summary: Humes confirms her range goes above the C she once stated and that her voice gets clearer as she warms up. Lyrics mean a lot to her, and a good pianist sometimes makes her stop singing and listen.

segments.title: Drummers: Ed Thigpen, Jo Jones and Cozy Cole
segments.summary: Ed Thigpen went abroad with Humes and lives in Europe, and his father was a good drummer. Humes calls Jo Jones her alma mater, and Cozy Cole sweet and reliable.

segments.title: Sid Catlett dies in her arms at a JATP concert
segments.summary: Backstage at a Jazz at the Philharmonic show, Sid Catlett was holding her, then collapsed and died as she walked away. The stage manager put her on stage next because he feared she would panic.

segments.title: Ornette Coleman and free-form playing
segments.summary: Dance asks about avant-garde players like Ornette Coleman and Sun Ra. Humes says she played with Coleman not long ago and thought he was good.

segments.title: Stanley Dance coaxes her into the Carnegie Hall Basie tribute
segments.summary: Dance turns to the 1972 comeback. Stanley Dance visited Louisville and urged her to sing in a Newport tribute to Basie at Carnegie Hall. She doubted herself, Nellie Lutcher calmed her backstage, and she was sensational.

segments.title: France within a month: Dr. Chavron and the 'Helen Comes Back' session
segments.summary: A month later she was in France for her first time in that way, meeting Dr. Chavron, touring for Monestier and recording for Black and Blue with Milt Buckner and Jay McShann, who was in good form.

segments.title: Stanley Dance gets credit for bringing her back
segments.summary: Dance says Stanley took the French recording to John Hammond at Columbia, and that Humes always credits Stanley Dance, not Hammond or Josephson, with coaxing her back. Humes recalls his all-night visit.

segments.title: 1974 return to France and New York, and her father's death
segments.summary: After a trip home she returned to France in 1974 for her own tour, then worked briefly at a New York club and Barney Josephson's New Year's Eve party. While she was there her father died.

segments.title: Packed opening at the Cookery and the rave reviews
segments.summary: She did the New Year's Eve show for Barney Josephson, and after she began at the Cookery she received big reviews. Returning from Louisville she found people lined up in the snow and Moe had to bring her in.

segments.title: Black and Blue's objection to her Montreux festival appearance
segments.summary: At Montreux in 1974 the Black and Blue people objected and brought an attorney, though Humes said she had no contract and would not sing her Black and Blue songs.

segments.title: Live recording at Montreux and European applause
segments.summary: Humes thought the Montreux live album was her worst and noisy, but she likes the sound of European audiences applauding and standing for her.

segments.title: Earl Hines forgot his own number at Montreux
segments.summary: Making the live record at Montreux, Earl Hines forgot his song 'You Can Depend on Me' and Humes had to sing the whole thing to him.

segments.title: The Armstrong tribute and the Rotterdam trip with Dizzy, Carmen and Brubeck
segments.summary: She and Dance date the Armstrong tribute to 1975 and the Rotterdam trip to 1976, with Dizzy Gillespie, Carmen McRae, Dave Brubeck, Wild Bill Davis, Floyd Smith and Buddy Rich.

segments.title: Kentucky Colonel and Distinguished Citizen of Louisville
segments.summary: Louisville made her a Kentucky Colonel, a captain of the Southern Belle and a Distinguished Citizen. She did not know about it beforehand. She now stays at a hotel in Louisville but plans to go back and stay home.

segments.title: Grammy nominations and Ella always winning
segments.summary: She was nominated by NARAS in 1980 for 'Sneakin' Around' and again in 1981 for the Muse album. She figures Ella will always win but is happy to be considered.

segments.title: 'Outskirts of Town' with Eddie Vinson and the old Rushing session finally issued
segments.summary: On the 1979-80 Muse album with Eddie 'Cleanhead' Vinson and Arnett Cobb she made up choruses and jokes. Columbia then issued for the first time a 1950s session she had made with Jimmy Rushing.

segments.title: Clubs and concerts: Concerts by the Sea, Toronto, Sandy's Jazz Revival
segments.summary: She lists West Coast and other bookings: Concerts by the Sea, the Lighthouse, UCLA, Max Cavalli's Canadian dates in Toronto, and Sandy's outside Boston.

segments.title: Room Full of Blues, Sandy's Place and Blues Alley
segments.summary: At Sandy's she first met the young band Room Full of Blues and told them to learn to read music; she heard them again at the Bottom Line. Sandy wants her back but she is sick, and she also plays Blues Alley in Washington.

segments.title: Illness and her 1980 operation
segments.summary: Feeling lousy, she kept going to hospitals until a nurse sent her to the right people. She had her operation on July 31, 1980 and was on her way to Japan a month later.

segments.title: First trip to Japan with Teddy Wilson, Milt Hinton and Shelly Manne
segments.summary: She went to Japan in August 1980 with a group including Benny Goodman, Teddy Wilson, Milt Hinton, Shelly Manne and Lockjaw. Audiences went crazy, Shirley Silver carried her bags, and she did three concerts in eight days.

segments.title: Two weeks at Ronnie Scott's in London
segments.summary: From Japan she went via New York to London for two weeks at Ronnie Scott's with English backing musicians, and saw Max Jones. She says she is not as close to the English as to the French.

segments.title: Recovering in Los Angeles, upcoming Disneyland and Cookery dates, and closing
segments.summary: Back in Los Angeles since December, she faces Disneyland dates and the Cookery on the 16th. She says working makes her feel better, and nobody can tell she was ill. The tape is switched off.
